verdict.rationale: The first clause is lexically decisive. Demonic reality is named with dense vocabulary: 'devil' (diabolos, G1228, 38 occurrences spread across the whole Bible), 'unclean spirit' (pneuma akatharton, G4151 with G0169, 32 occurrences of akathartos meaning 'unclean'), and concrete narrative expulsion, namely 'to cast out' (ekballo) paired with 'demon' (daimonion), G1544 with G1140, co-occurring in 23 verses across the Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) and Acts, while Mark 9:25 to 29 records Jesus rebuking and commanding 'come out' (exelthe, an aorist imperative, a completed past-action command form) and then saying 'this kind' (touto to genos) can come out by nothing except 'in prayer' (en proseuche). The believer response in the epistles is named with 'resist' (anthistemi, G0436, 14 occurrences spanning Romans, Galatians, Ephesians, James, 1 Peter), 'be sober' (nepho, G3525, 6 occurrences all in vigilance contexts), and 'be watchful' (gregoreo, G1127, 23 occurrences) plus 'submit yourselves' (hypotasso, G5293, 40 occurrences) at James 4:7. The second clause, that routinizing deliverance and locating a demon behind every sin and trauma is unbalanced, is an evaluative inference. The Sceva episode (Acts 19) and Matthew 7:22 supply strong negative cases against using the name as a formula, and the canon prescribes no standing technique, but the vocabulary illustrates rather than legislates the frequency judgment, so the aggregate sits as disputed.

scripture.reasoning: Jesus 'rebuked' (epetimesen, a completed past action of the verb epitimao) the 'unclean spirit' (pneuma to akatharton), addresses it as the 'mute and deaf spirit' (to alalon kai kophon pneuma), and commands 'come out of him and enter him no more' (exelthe ex autou kai meketi eiselthes eis auton). The aorist imperative (a completed-action command form) plus prohibition encodes a direct one-event authoritative command, not a recurring procedure. The verb 'mute' (alalos, G0216) is a Markan cluster of three occurrences, descriptive of the manifestation, not of a method.

'This kind can come out by nothing except by prayer' (Touto to genos en oudeni dynatai exelthein ei me en proseuche). The prepositional phrase 'in prayer' (en proseuche) locates the remedy in dependence on God, not in a transmissible technique. The disciples' earlier failure, 'they were not able' (ouk ischysan, Mark 9:18), grounds the lexical point: prior commissioning does not guarantee mechanical efficacy.

'I told your disciples to cast it out and they were not able' (Eipa tois mathetais sou hina auto ekbalosin kai ouk ischysan). The aorist subjunctive (completed-action 'that they might' form) 'they should cast out' (ekbalosin) paired with 'they were not able' (ouk ischysan) registers that the act exists as a real category yet is not a guaranteed-output procedure. This undercuts any mechanistic frequency claim from inside the same pericope (story unit).

'For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places' (Hoti ouk estin hemin he pale pros haima kai sarka alla pros tas archas, pros tas exousias, pros tous kosmokratoras tou skotous toutou, pros ta pneumatika tes ponerias en tois epouraniois). The hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) 'wrestling' (pale, G3823, only here) and the hapax 'world-ruler' (kosmokrator, G2888, only here) frame an organized spiritual opposition. The accumulation of rank terms supports clause one (real demonic activity), but the prescriptive verses that follow (6:13 to 18) name 'full armor' (panoplia, G3833, breastplate, shield, helmet, sword) and 'prayer' (proseuche), not 'to cast out' (ekballo) or any expulsion verb.

'Submit yourselves therefore to God, but resist the devil, and he will flee from you' (Hypotagete oun to theo, antistete de to diabolo, kai pheuxetai aph hymon). The paired aorist passive imperative (a completed-action passive command form) 'submit yourselves' (hypotagete) and aorist active imperative (a completed-action active command form) 'resist' (antistete) prescribe the believer response to the 'devil' (diabolos) as submission to God and resistance, with the future 'he will flee' (pheuxetai) as outcome. The verbs are ordinary discipleship verbs, 'submit' (hypotasso, G5293, 40 occurrences) and 'resist' (anthistemi, G0436, 14 occurrences spread across the New Testament), not specialized expulsion vocabulary.

'Be sober, be watchful, your adversary the devil walks about like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour' (Nepsate, gregoresate, ho antidikos hymon diabolos hos leon oryomenos peripatei zeton tina katapiein). The aorist imperatives (completed-action command forms) 'be sober' (nepho, G3525, 6 occurrences, every one a vigilance command in 1 Thessalonians, 2 Timothy, 1 Peter) and 'be watchful' (gregoreo, G1127, 23 occurrences spanning the Synoptic Gospels, Pauline letters, Revelation) describe the normative posture toward the 'devil' (diabolos) as sobriety and watchfulness, not routine expulsion.

'Whom resist, steadfast in the faith' (Ho antistete stereoi te pistei). The same 'resist' (anthistemi) as James 4:7, paired with 'steadfast in the faith' (stereoi te pistei), marks the believer response as resistance grounded in steadfast faith. The cross-letter agreement between James and 1 Peter on 'resist the devil' (antistete to diabolo) is the strongest lexical signal that the apostolic prescription is steady resistance rather than a frequency-driven program.

'Preaching in their synagogues throughout all Galilee and casting out demons' (Kerysson eis tas synagogas auton eis holen ten Galilaian kai ta daimonia ekballon). The participial (verb form acting as adjective or modifier) 'casting out' (ekballon) is paired with 'preaching' (kerysson), locating expulsion alongside proclamation in Jesus' mission. The 'cast out' (ekballo) plus 'demon' (daimonion) idiom co-occurs in 23 verses across the Synoptic Gospels and Acts, establishing the act as a real lexical category quite apart from any frequency rule.

Paul commands the 'spirit of Python' (pneuma Pythona) 'to come out of her' (exelthein ap autes) 'in the name of Jesus Christ' (en onomati Iesou Christou), and it leaves 'at that very hour' (auto te hora). The aorist infinitive (completed-action 'to' verb form) 'to come out' (exelthein) plus the prepositional phrase 'in the name' (en onomati) grounds the expulsion in the named Christ. This is the apostolic precedent that demonic activity may be answered by direct deliverance when the case is genuinely manifest, but the narrative also marks it as an episodic response to a public manifestation, not a scheduled rite.

complicating_texts.resolution: The itinerant 'exorcists' (exorkistai, G1845, a true hapax meaning a word occurring only once in the entire Bible) 'undertook' (epecheiresan, G2021, three New Testament occurrences and all of an undertaking that miscarries) to invoke the 'name' (onoma) of the Lord Jesus as a borrowed formula. The lexical choice marks them as outsiders adopting a technique, and the verb of attempting telegraphs failure. This is the strongest internal warrant for the second clause: it shows the name deployed as a transferable formula by those without standing fails.

The 'evil spirit' (pneuma to poneron) answers 'Jesus I know and Paul I am acquainted with, but who are you?' (ton Iesoun ginosko kai ton Paulon epistamai, hymeis de tines este), and the possessed man overpowers them so they flee 'naked' (gymnous, G1131, naked) 'and wounded' (kai tetraumatismenous). The narrative outcome embeds the abuse-and-danger warning directly in the text, supplying the canonical basis for calling routinized deliverance unbalanced. Resolved as illustrative.

Speakers protest 'in your name we cast out demons' (to so onomati daimonia exebalomen), and Jesus answers 'I never knew you' (ouk egnon hymas). The aorist (completed past action) 'we cast out' (exebalomen) shows that casting out demons in Jesus' name may be claimed by those whom Christ disowns, so the activity by itself, separated from a real relation to Christ, is not a sign of standing. This is the second strongest internal warrant for the caution clause.

The pastoral epistles list 'overseer' (episkopos), 'deacon' (diakonos), 'elder' (presbyteros) and gifts but contain no 'exorcist' (exorkistes) office and no instruction to institute one. The absence is lexical: there is no office word for the role. Absence is suggestive of the caution clause but is not a positive prescription, so it remains an inferential rather than decisive datum, unresolved on its own.

'And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons' (Tois pisteusasin de tauta parakolouthesei, en to onomati mou daimonia ekbalousin). The future 'they will cast out' (ekbalousin) attaches expulsion to believers, but the verse sits in the longer ending of Mark which the manuscript tradition transmits unevenly. The act is still attested undisputedly across Mark 1:34, Mark 1:39, Matthew 10:8, and Acts 16:18, so the warrant for clause one does not depend on this verse, and the variant exposure does not move the aggregate.

variant_units_examined.note: Mark 16:17 sits in the longer ending (Mark 16:9 to 20), text-critically contested. Because Mark 1:34, Mark 1:39, Matthew 10:8, and Acts 16:18 carry the act of casting out demons undisputedly, the contested status of Mark 16:17 does not alter the aggregate verdict, hence minor.

Some witnesses add 'and fasting' (kai nesteia) to 'in prayer' (en proseuche). The addition does not change the lexical point that the remedy is named in a prepositional phrase of dependence on God rather than as a technique, so the verdict is unaffected.

variants.note: The anchor verses lie outside the published critical edition of New Testament textual variants (ECM) window, which currently covers 3 John 1:1 to 1:15. The longer ending of Mark and the 'and fasting' (kai nesteia) variant in Mark 9:29 are well-known and noted, but neither moves the aggregate because the warrant is multiply attested elsewhere.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the gospels and Acts as a continuing pattern: 'cast out' (ekballo) plus 'demon' (daimonion) as a live category, Mark 16:17 (with text-critical asterisks) as warrant, and Acts 16:18 as apostolic precedent. The first clause of the proposition is affirmed straightforwardly. The second clause is read as legitimately cautioning against unauthorized formulas (Sceva in Acts 19, Matthew 7:22) but some lineages within this lens do treat habitual sin and trauma as frequently demonic, so the evaluative second half is not uniformly accepted, leaving the aggregate disputed within the lens itself.

Reads Ephesians 6:12 as a programmatic, ongoing spiritual conflict with named adversary ranks ('rulers' (archai), 'authorities' (exousiai), 'world-rulers' (kosmokratores)), and the gospel and Acts expulsion idiom as paradigmatic for a standing pastoral practice. Within this lens, treating routine deliverance as unbalanced is itself unbalanced because the danger of underdiagnosis is real. The proposition is therefore contested from this side.

Affirms demonic reality from 'devil' (diabolos, G1228, 38 occurrences) and the gospel narratives while reading the absence of any prescribed standing rite, the 'full armor' (panoplia) plus 'prayer' (proseuche) prescription in Ephesians 6:13 to 18, the Sceva warning, and Matthew 7:22 as direct support for both halves of the proposition. The first clause is affirmed by occasional pastoral care including prayer (Mark 9:29 'in prayer' (en proseuche)); the second clause is affirmed by the absence of an 'exorcist' (exorkistes) office and by the negative cases.

Holds that Scripture attests both real expulsion and real danger of misuse, with the apostolic prescription being submission, resistance, sobriety, watchfulness, steadfast faith, and prayer (James 4:7, 1 Peter 5:8 to 9). The proposition mirrors that synthesis: yes to demonic reality and occasional prayerful deliverance, no to a frequency-driven program that diagnoses a demon behind every sin and trauma.

hermeneutics.notes: Both halves draw on 'analogy of Scripture' (analogia scripturae, reading Scripture with Scripture), holding narrative deliverance accounts together with the epistolary resistance commands. Lenses converge on clause one (demonic reality is real, prayerful response to genuine cases is legitimate) and diverge on clause two (whether the lexical pattern materially supports calling routinization unbalanced, or whether that judgment imports a prudential rule the vocabulary does not legislate). The divergence on clause two is what keeps the aggregate verdict disputed.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: What does the canonical vocabulary, 'devil' (diabolos), 'demon' (daimonion), 'unclean spirit' (pneuma akatharton), 'to cast out' (ekballo), 'come out' (exelthe), 'in prayer' (en proseuche), 'resist' (anthistemi), 'submit' (hypotasso), 'be sober' (nepho), 'be watchful' (gregoreo), show about whether demonic activity is real, whether believers may respond with prayer for deliverance, and whether the canon prescribes, permits, or leaves open a routine, technique-driven deliverance ministry that attributes sin and trauma to demonic causes by default?
stem_audit.notes: The original stem encodes an evaluative verdict in two phrases: routinized deliverance ministry that locates a demon behind every sin and trauma, and is unbalanced. Both are conclusions, not neutral descriptions. The verdict is derived on the original stem, but the neutralized form was used to test whether the lexical pattern matches the evaluative half. The lexicon supports the warrant for clause one and lends real but not decisive weight to clause two through negative cases (Sceva in Acts 19, Matthew 7:22) and the absence of an 'exorcist' (exorkistes) office word in the pastoral epistles.

lay_summary: Scripture plainly treats evil spirits as real and uses dense vocabulary for them. The word 'devil' (diabolos) occurs thirty-eight times across Revelation, John, Peter, James, Hebrews, the Pastoral Epistles, and Acts. The phrase 'to cast out demons' (ekballo plus daimonion) co-occurs in twenty-three verses across Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Acts. In Mark 9 a boy is afflicted by an unclean mute spirit, the disciples cannot drive it out, and Jesus rebukes it and commands it to come out and not return, then tells the disciples this kind comes out by nothing except by prayer (en proseuche). Acts 16:18 records Paul commanding a spirit to come out in the name of Jesus Christ, and it leaves at once. So the first half of the proposition, that demonic activity is real and that prayer for deliverance can be a real pastoral need, rests on clear words across many books. The second half is a wisdom inference. James 4:7 and 1 Peter 5:8 to 9 prescribe the normal believer response with everyday discipleship verbs: submit (hypotasso), resist (anthistemi), be sober (nepho), be watchful (gregoreo), stand firm in faith. Ephesians 6:12 frames the conflict spiritually with the once-only words 'wrestling' (pale) and 'world-ruler' (kosmokrator), but the verses that follow tell the reader to put on the full armor (panoplia) and to pray, not to perform a casting-out procedure. The pastoral epistles list overseer, deacon, and elder as offices but include no exorcist office. Acts 19 sharpens the warning: itinerant exorcists who use the name of Jesus as a borrowed formula are overpowered by an evil spirit and flee naked and wounded. Matthew 7:22 sharpens it further: some will claim to have cast out demons in Jesus' name and yet hear, I never knew you. Together these warn that successful-looking expulsion language is not by itself proof of standing. The vocabulary supports calling routinization unbalanced, but the canon does not state a rule on frequency, so faithful readers divide on the evaluative half. The first half is decisively grounded, the second is a wise reading of the emphasis, and the aggregate verdict is recorded as disputed.
